title: TB8-04603
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Associate Appellants), citizens of Jamaica, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 16, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Associate Appellants), citizens of Jamaica, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 16, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants request that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) substitute a decision that they are Convention refugees or, in the alternative, that the matter by referred back to the RPD for a de novo assessment.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.

The Appellants' refugee claim is based upon the sexual orientation of the Principal Appellant. The Principal Appellant alleges that she is a lesbian who has suffered a variety of discriminatory and abusive encounters in Jamaica based upon her sexual orientation.1 She alleges that she had one long-term serious relationship with a woman in Jamaica who was attacked and ultimately fled to the United States.2 The Principal Appellant alleges that her situation deteriorated after rumours of her sexual orientation spread around Jamaica due to a picture on social media.3 As a result of this, the Appellants fled to Canada and brought their claims for protection.

The RPD heard the Appellants' claims on July 13, 2017 and rejected them in a decision dated August 16, 2017.4 The RPD found that the Principal Appellant had not credibly established her sexual orientation on the basis of inconsistencies, vagueness, a lack of relevant corroborative documentation, and a lack of subjective fear.5 The decision was communicated to the Appellants in a Notice of Decision dated February 15, 2018.6 The Appellants allege that the RPD erred in the following manner: (a) The RPD gave too much weight to the inconsistency in the attack on the Principal Appellant's alleged partner; (b) The RPD erred by rejecting reasonable explanations for the lack of testimony from the Principal Appellant's husband and same-sex partner; (c) The RPD misapprehended the Principal Appellant's testimony and failed to apply the SOGIE Guideline7 in assessing a lack of documentation from the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner; and (d) The RPD erred in concluding that the Principal Appellant lacked subjective fear based upon reavailment and delay in departure.

In addition, the Appellants argue that new evidence further demonstrates the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation and that the Associate Appellants are at risk based upon the sexual orientation of their mother, the Principal Appellant.

The Appellants submitted a number of pieces of new evidence at various points in the appeal process. These include: (a) An affidavit of the Principal Appellant, sworn March 23, 2018, submitted with the appeal record and attaching the following: (i) A letter, photographs and text messages from the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner in Canada; (ii) A letter from a friend in Canada who is aware of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation; (iii) A letter from an employee of the 519 confirming the Principal Appellant's continued involvement with the organization; (b) An affidavit of the Principal Appellant, received December 10, 2018, confirming her divorce from her husband and attaching proof of the divorce; and (c) A letter from the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner in Canada confirming that the relationship with the Principal Appellant had ended. This letter was submitted in May, 2019, in response to the RAD's request that the same-sex partner testify at a hearing.

For the reasons that follow, I am admitting the evidence from the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner as new evidence, and I convened an oral hearing on the basis of the first letter, photographs and text messages. As will be explained in this decision, this evidence and the testimony elicited at the hearing is dispositive of this appeal. Accordingly, it is not necessary for me to determine the admissibility of the other pieces of proposed new evidence because they do not impact on the outcome of the appeal.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the persons who are the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that the persons could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection of their refugee claims. If the proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4), I must assess, pursuant to the Federal Court of Appeal's decisions in Raza8 and Singh,9 the newness, credibility and relevance of the evidence in order to determine whether it is admissible. Additionally, for evidence submitted after the perfection of the appeal, I must consider the requirements of Rule 29(4) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules.

Turning first to the initial letter, dated March 5, 2018, from the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner.10 The letter writer, Ms. T.T., had previously provided evidence in the Appellants' RPD claim that she was a friend of the Principal Appellant who was also a sexual minority, and she knew of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation.11 The Principal Appellant alleges that, after her claim was rejected, her relationship with her partner who was living in the United States deteriorated, and they broke up.12 She alleges that, after this, the relationship with T.T. went from platonic to romantic in approximately XXXX 2017.13 T.T. confirms this in her letter, and the Principal Appellant affirms that T.T. is willing to appear before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) to speak about the relationship.14 Along with the letter, the Appellants submitted two photographs of the Principal Appellant with T.T. from February 2018 and WhatsApp messages from March 2018.15

I find that this evidence is admissible and that it meets the requirements to convene an oral hearing. First, I find that the evidence post-dates the rejection of the claim. The RPD's decision was signed on August 16, 2017. The relationship between the Principal Appellant and T.T. only became romantic at this time, as the Principal Appellant affirms that the relationship only started after the rejection of her claim and the breakdown of the relationship with her past partner.16 Therefore, the evidence post-dates the rejection of the claim and meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

Looking at the jurisprudential factors, the evidence meets the low threshold of credibility for admission in that there are no prima facie deficiencies and is relevant in that it is capable of proving that the Principal Appellant had a same-sex relationship, a fact that is germane to the question of sexual orientation and the claim overall. Finally, the evidence is new in that the relationship only developed around the time the claim was rejected and therefore goes to a fact that was unknown to the Appellants at the time of the RPD hearing. Therefore, I find the evidence meets the jurisprudential requirements.

I also find that the requirements to convene a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA are met. The allegation of a new relationship raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Principal Appellant; it is central to the decision, as it goes directly to the issue of sexual orientation and, as will be discussed below, if accepted, would justify allowing the refugee protection claim.

I also admit into evidence the second letter written by T.T., which was submitted in May, 2019. This letter was written in response to the notice of hearing sent out by the RAD which requested T.T. to appear as a witness at the hearing. Counsel for the Appellants notified the RAD that the Principal Appellant and T.T.'s relationship had ended on poor terms, and T.T. refused to appear as a witness but had agreed to provide a letter.17 Given that this letter was submitted in response to a direction from the RAD, I find that it meets rule 29, in that the Appellants could not have provided it until the request by the RAD was made. I also find it to be relevant, probative and new, as it goes to the genuineness of the relationship and the evolution of the relationship from the time of the rejection of the claim to present. For the same reasons, I find that the evidence meets subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Additionally, I find that the evidence meets the jurisprudential requirements for the reasons given above, with regard to the other evidence about the relationship with T.T. Therefore, I am admitting the second T.T. letter into evidence.

When reviewing the RPD's decision, the RAD is required to independently assess whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of fact, law or mixed fact and law.18 I may defer to the RPD on a finding of credibility on oral evidence where the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances. In this instance, as I admitted new evidence and convened an oral hearing on this basis, I am conducting an independent assessment of this evidence, which forms the basis of my decision.

The Appellants raised a number of issues with regard to the RPD's decision. In my view, some have merit and others do not. However, in my view, it is not necessary to address the RPD's decision and the Appellants' arguments about it, as they are not determinative of the appeal. I have before me new evidence that was not before the RPD. As I will discuss below, the evidence establishes that the Principal Appellant was in a genuine same-sex relationship in Canada, on a balance of probabilities. In my view, this is sufficient reliable evidence upon which to conclude that the Principal Appellant is a sexual minority. Therefore, it is not necessary for me to determine if the RPD erred in its conclusions below because, even if the RPD did not err in its individual findings, this new evidence is determinative of the appeal and is sufficient for me to substitute a decision. I will address the issues as follows: (a) The Principal Appellant has established that she is a sexual minority based upon new evidence submitted on appeal; and (b) The Appellants are Convention refugees on the basis of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation. The Principal Appellant has established that she is a sexual minority based upon new evidence submitted on appeal
For the following reasons, I find that the Appellants have established that the Principal Appellant is a sexual minority on the basis of new evidence submitted on appeal.

As discussed above, the Appellants submitted new evidence in support of their appeal which alleged that the Principal Appellant had a same-sex relationship in Canada. This evidence included: two letters from the same-sex partner, text messages and photographs. A hearing was convened on the basis of this evidence. Initially, I requested that the partner, T.T., appear as a witness at the hearing, as the Principal Appellant indicated T.T. was "willing to appear" before the Board to speak about the relationship.19 However, after the hearing was convened, the Appellants informed the Board that the Principal Appellant's relationship with T.T. had ended on poor terms, and T.T. was unwilling to appear at the hearing and, ultimately, that T.T. had agreed to provide a second letter.20 The hearing proceeded with the Principal Appellant testifying about the relationship. This made an evaluation of the credibility of the relationship more challenging, as it is more straightforward to assess the genuineness of a relationship when both partners are present and can testify, and the consistency of their testimony can be assessed, as opposed to where one person is giving evidence which is largely uncorroborated.

It is important to set out that this process led to some questions about the credibility of this relationship. It is clear under the SOGIE Guideline that corroborative evidence is often not available in cases involving sexual minorities and that this should not be held against a refugee claimant, where reasonable explanations are provided for the lack of corroboration.21 Indeed, it is common to proceed by questioning an individual about a past relationship without the partner appearing as a witness or even providing a letter or affidavit of support. However, there is a difference between an allegation about a past relationship where the partner lives in a different country, where being a sexual minority is risky, and an allegation of a current or recently past relationship where the partner lives in Canada. In the latter case, it may be more reasonable to expect the partner to testify at the hearing. This is more-so where the partner has indicated a willingness to do so, as was the case here.22

I considered that the Principal Appellant's relationship had ended badly. However, the Appellants indicated that T.T. had made a refugee claim in Canada on the basis of her sexual orientation, and acknowledged in testimony that T.T. would understand the importance of having a witness at a refugee claim or appeal.23 Additionally, this is not the first time that the Principal Appellant had a same-sex partner who would logically have been available to testify and failed to do so. At the time of her RPD hearing, the Principal Appellant alleged she had a partner in the United States, but failed to produce her as a witness. Accordingly, I had to consider whether this was a pattern of the Principal Appellant being disingenuous in presenting alleged same-sex partners. After hearing the Principal Appellant testify, I conclude that this was not the case and that the Principal Appellant was genuinely in the relationship with T.T., regardless of T.T.'s feelings, for several reasons.

First, the Principal Appellant clearly understood the importance of having T.T. testify at the hearing and gave evidence about the considerable efforts she took to get her to appear in conjunction with evidence about the breakdown of the relationship. The Principal Appellant testified that problems in the relationship occurred because T.T. wanted to be more open, but the Principal Appellant is still hiding her sexual orientation from her children.24 She explained that when T.T. came to her home, she made T.T. sleep on the couch, which upset T.T.25 She also explained other steps she took to make T.T. feel valued in the relationship despite her unwillingness to tell her children, including paying T.T.'s rent, buying her lots of things, and taking steps to include T.T. as an insurance beneficiary on her work policy.26 The Principal Appellant explained that this last effort ultimately made the situation worse, as T.T. was unhappy when the Principal Appellant refused to make her the first beneficiary, ahead of her children.27 This anecdote was spontaneous and had the ring of truth to it.

Additionally, the Principal Appellant explained that, after the relationship ended because T.T. was unfaithful and returned to another partner, the Principal Appellant tried to reach out to her unsuccessfully.28 She explained that, after the RAD hearing was convened, she tried calling T.T. both at home and work, but that her number had been blocked from T.T.'s phone, and T.T. hung up on her at work.29 The Principal Appellant explained that she went to T.T.'s work, but T.T. still refused to testify, and it was only the Principal Appellant's lawyer who finally convinced T.T. to write the second letter.30 I asked the Principal Appellant whether she and her lawyer considered asking the Board to issue a summons for T.T. to appear, and she testified that her lawyer had raised this possibility with her, but given how T.T. was acting, she felt that if T.T. were forced to appear, she would act poorly or sabotage the hearing.31 All of this evidence demonstrates that the Principal Appellant took the importance of T.T.'s testimony very seriously, and this was more than a relationship entered into for the purpose of bolstering the refugee claim. It also demonstrated a level of detailed knowledge which spoke to a genuine relationship.

Beyond this, the Principal Appellant's evidence about T.T. and their relationship was consistent with the evidence in her affidavit and T.T.'s letters. She gave details to the photos and text messages provided on appeal. However, it was not this consistency and detail which was the most convincing evidence. It was the Principal Appellant's emotion in discussing the relationship, and particularly the breakdown of the relationship. As explained above, she testified to the efforts she took to make T.T. happy and her genuine shock when T.T. ended things in such a quick and dramatic fashion. She explained how the end started with a fight after T.T. told her she was going to bed but then the Principal Appellant found out she was still online. The Principal Appellant explained this was when she began to believe T.T. was talking to someone else. She explained how she tried to do anything she could to show T.T. she was serious, including paying her rent, to the point where she nearly went bankrupt. She was emotional. This evidence demonstrated that whatever T.T.'s motives for the relationship were, the Principal Appellant was genuinely committed to her.

For these reasons, I find that the Principal Appellant has established that she was in a genuine relationship with T.T., on a balance of probabilities, and, as a result, she is a sexual minority. The Appellants are Convention refugees on the basis of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation

For the following reasons, I find that the Appellants are Convention refugees on the basis of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation. For the Principal Appellant, this is based upon her membership in a particular social group of sexual minorities, and for the Associate Appellants, this is based upon their membership in a particular social group of minor children of sexual minorities. I also find that the Appellants do not have access to adequate state protection or a viable internal flight alternative.

The documentary evidence in the most recent National Documentation Package (NDP) shows that same-sex relations are criminalized; there are no antidiscrimination laws to protect LGBTI persons, and the law "legitimizes violence towards LGBTI persons."32 Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) report an increase of discrimination against sexual minorities as well as acts of violence.33 These acts of violence include physical, verbal and sexual assault, threats, extortion, home invasion, robbery, burglary, vandalism and mob attacks.34 On this basis, I find that the Principal Appellant faces more than a mere possibility of persecution on the basis of her sexual orientation. Given that the Associate Appellants are minors (at the time of claiming) and reside with their mother, I find that these risks are also faced by them, particularly the risks of home invasion, robbery or mob attack. Therefore, I find that the Associate Appellants face more than a mere possibility of persecution based upon their family status. These are both particular social groups contemplated by the Convention.

With regard to state protection, there have been some efforts of political leaders to change the culture as well as a prohibition of discrimination in police policy, but despite this, documents show that Jamaica remains generally homophobic with a "culture of outward hostility toward LGBTI individuals."35 Government agencies are often involved in acts of discrimination against sexual minorities, and there continue to be reports of police abuse, as well as police violations of the rights of those in the LGBT community.36 Additionally, there have been reports of inaction by police where reports have been made to them.37 Accordingly, I find that there is not adequate state protection for the Appellants on an operational level. I also find that there is no viable internal flight alternative, given the size of Jamaica, the fact that state actors are involved in the persecution of sexual minorities and given that country conditions, as described above, are present across the nation.
For these reasons, I find that the Appellants are Convention refugees.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its own determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
